exam_data <- read_csv("../data/Exam_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

title: Hands-On Exercise4
text:
3 Visualizing Distribution with Ridgeline Plot
A ridgeline plot (also known as a Joyplot) is a visualization technique used to display the distribution of a numeric variable across multiple groups. These distributions can be shown as histograms or density curves, all aligned to a common horizontal axis and slightly overlapping to highlight differences between groups.
Ridgeline plots are most effective when you need to display distributions across a medium to large number of groups. In such cases, traditional side‑by‑side plots would consume too much space, whereas the overlapping layout of ridgelines makes more efficient use of the plotting area.
For datasets with fewer than five groups, other distribution plots (such as boxplots or violin plots) are usually clearer. Ridgeline plots also work best when there is a distinct pattern or ranking among groups. Without such structure, the overlapping curves can create visual clutter, making the plot harder to interpret and less insightful.

3.1 Plotting Ridgeline Graph using ggridges method.
The ggridges package provides two primary geoms for creating ridgeline plots:
geom_ridgeline(): draws ridgelines directly from supplied height values.
geom_density_ridges(): first estimates the data’s density and then uses those values to construct ridgelines.
We will try using the geom_density_ridges()

The plotThe code chunk











Each pink ridge represents the distribution of English grades for a different class, showing how scores vary across groups. Classes 3A and 3C have higher grade concentrations toward the upper end, while class 3I and 3H show broader spreads with lower average grades.


ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = lighten("#f28fa3", 0.3),
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English Grades",
    expand = c(0,0)
    ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2,2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()





3.2 Varying fill colors along the x-axis
Sometimes, instead of filling the area beneath a ridgeline with a single solid color, we may want the fill to vary along the x‑axis. This effect can be achieved using geom_ridgeline_gradient() or geom_density_ridges_gradient(). These geoms function like geom_ridgeline() and geom_density_ridges(), but they allow for changing fill colors across the plot.
One limitation is that they do not support alpha transparency in the fill. For technical reasons, we can either apply varying colors or transparency, but not both simultaneously.

The plotThe code chunk











The color gradient from purple to yellow represents temperature values in °F, depicts how grade distributions vary.


ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = after_stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Temp. [F]", option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "English Grades",
    expand = c(0,0)
    ) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, expand = expansion(add = c(0.2,2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()





3.3 Mapping the probabilities directly onto color
Beyond offering additional geom objects for ridgeline plots, the ggridges package also introduces a statistical transformation called stat_density_ridges(), which serves as a replacement for ggplot2’s standard stat_density().
The figure below demonstrates this approach by mapping probabilities calculated with stat(ecdf), representing the empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) of English scores. This allows the ridgeline plot to display cumulative probabilities rather than raw densities, giving a different perspective on the distribution.

The plotThe code chunk











The color gradient from yellow to dark purple represents tail probability, showing how likely extreme scores are within each class. Darker areas indicate lower probabilities at the distribution tails.


ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5-stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()
When using stat_density_ridges(), it is important to include the argument calc_ecdf = TRUE. This ensures that the function computes the empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) for the data, allowing the ridgeline plot to represent cumulative probabilities rather than just densities. Without this argument, the plot will not display the ecdf correctly.
Setting direction = -1 flips the color scale, so the colors are mapped in the opposite way





3.4 Ridgeline plots with quantile lines
Using geom_density_ridges_gradient(), ridgeline plots can be colored according to quantiles by mapping the aesthetic stat(quantile). This approach highlights different portions of the distribution with distinct colors, making it easier to see how values fall into quantile ranges.
The figure below demonstrates this technique, where the ridgelines are shaded by quantile rather than a single uniform fill.

The plotThe code chunk











Each curve is divided into quartiles, colored from dark purple (lowest scores) to yellow (highest), showing how student performance varies within and across classes.


ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = factor(stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE,
                      quantiles = 4,
                      quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()



Instead of defining quantiles by number, we can also set them using cut points. For example, the 2.5% and 97.5% tails to color the ridgeline plot, as shown in the figure below.

The plotThe code chunk











The shaded regions represent probability intervals—red for the lower tail (0–2.5%), gray for the central range (2.5–97.5%), and blue for the upper tail (97.5–100%). This highlights how each class’ scores spread and where extreme values occur within their distributions.


ggplot(exam_data,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = factor(stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE,
                      quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#FF0000A0", "#A0A0A0A0", "#0000FFA0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) + 
  theme_ridges()
The stat_density_ridges chunk draws ridgelines with gradient fill, computes ecdf and marks the 2.5% and 97.5% quantile cut points. Then the scale_fill_manual chunk define custom colors and legends for the three quantile ranges.

title: Hands-On Exercise4
text:
4 Visualizing Distribution with Raincloud Plot
A raincloud plot is a visualization technique that combines a half‑density curve with a distribution plot. Its name comes from the density curve’s resemblance to a raincloud. Unlike a traditional boxplot, which does not reveal where values cluster, the raincloud plot highlights multiple modes in the data, making it easier to detect potential groupings.
In this section, we will learn how to create a raincloud plot to show the distribution of English scores by race, using functions from the ggdist and ggplot2 packages.

4.1 Plotting a Half Eye Graph
We will plot a Half Eye graph using stat_halfeye() from the ggdist package.

The plotThe code chunk











This half‑eye plot shows the distribution of English scores across four racial groups. Each gray half‑density curve represents how scores are spread within a group, with wider sections indicating where scores are more concentrated and narrower parts showing less frequent values.


ggplot(exam_data,
       aes( x = RACE,
            y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_color = NA)

adjust controls the smoothness of the density estimate.
justification shifts the half-eye slightly to avoid overlap with the boxplot or points.
.width disables inter bands meaning only the density curve is shown.
point_color removes individual data points from the plot.






4.2 Adding the boxplot using geom_boxplot()
We will add the second geometry layer using geom_boxplot() from ggplot2.

The plotThe code chunk











These boxplots show the median, interquartile range, and whiskers for English scores. It provides a clear summary of central tendency and spread, also the full distribution shape.


ggplot(exam_data,
       aes( x = RACE,
            y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_color = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.20,
  outlier.shape = NA)

width makes the boxplot narrow so it doesn’t dominate the density shape.
outlier.shape controls how outliers are displayed. NA in this case removes all outliers so they won’t be plotted.

Another setting that we can include in the geom_boxplot is alpha where it sets the opacity of the boxplot.





4.3 Adding the Dot Plots using stat_dots()
Next, we will add the third geometry layer using stat_dots(). This function creates a half-dotplot, which works like a histogram by showing the number of samples in dots in each bin.

The plot











The dots represent individual English scores, giving a clear view of data density, outliers, and summary statistics. ### The code chunk
ggplot(exam_data,
       aes( x = RACE,
            y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_color = NA) +
   geom_boxplot(width = 0.20, 
                outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left",
            justification = 1.2,
            binwidth = 0.5,
            dotsize = 2)

side = left instructs that we want it on the left-hand side of the boxplot.






4.4 Finishing touch
The coord_flip() flips the aces so the raincloud plot is displayed horizontally. This orientiation gives the plot its characteristic raincloud appearance, with the density curve above the boxplot. The theme_economist() applies a style from the ggthemes package.

The plotThe code chunk











This final plot combines the previous plots into a single plot that highlights each group’s characteristics.


ggplot(exam_data,
       aes( x = RACE,
            y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_color = NA) +
   geom_boxplot(width = 0.20, 
                outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left",
            justification = 1.2,
            binwidth = 0.5,
            dotsize = 1.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_economist()

5 Visual Statistical Analysis
In this section, we will practice using three packages for enhanced statistical visualization:

ggstatsplot: to create plots enriched with statistical details.
performance: to visualize model diagnostics.
parameters: to display and interpret model parameters.

Together, these tools provide a comprehensive way to explore data, assess models, and present results clearly.

5.1 Visual Statistical Analysis using ggstatsplot()
The ggstatsplot() package extends ggplot2 by including results from statistical tests directly into plots, making them more informative. It provides alternative inference methods by default like robust tests. Moreover, it also follows best practices for statistical reporting, with outputs formatted according to the APA gold standard.
For example, a robust t‑test result is automatically displayed in the plot with proper APA style notation.

title: Hands-On Exercise4
text:
6 Getting started

6.1 Check, install and launch packages
ggstatsplot and tidyverse will be used for this section exercise

pacman:: p_load(ggstatsplot,tidyverse)



6.2 One-sample test using gghistostats() method
We will use a visual of one-sample t-test on English scores using the gghistostats() function

The plotThe code chunk











This histogram shows the distribution of English scores with most values clustering between roughly 50 and 85. The blue dashed line marks the estimated mean score.


set.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam_data,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English scores"
)
set.seed() fixes the random seed so results are reproducible which is important for Bayesian sampling.
gghistostats() creates a histogram with statistical results.
type specifies a Bayesian one-sample test.
test.value compares the sample mean of English scores against the reference value.
xlab labels the x-axis as English scores for clarity.
By default, it provides statistical details, Bayes Factor, sample size and distribution summary.





6.3 Unpacking the Bayes Factor

A Bayes factor compares how likely the data are under one hypothesis versus another. It serves as a measure of the strength of evidence supporting one theory over its competitor.
This works because the Bayes factor allows us to evaluate evidence for the null hypothesis while incorporating prior information. In essence, it shows the weight of evidence favoring a particular hypothesis.
When testing two competing hypotheses, H₁ (the alternative) and H₀ (the null), the Bayes factor is often written as B₁₀, and is defined mathematically as the ratio of their likelihoods. A picture below is the mathematical formula  The Schwarz criterion (also known as the Bayesian Information Criterion, BIC) provides a straightforward way to approximate the Bayes Factor.



6.4 How to intepret Bayes Factor
A Bayes Factor can take any positive value. One widely used interpretation comes from Harold Jeffreys (1961), later refined by Lee and Wagenmakers (2013). Their framework provides a scale for judging the strength of evidence, where different ranges of Bayes Factor values correspond to varying levels of support for one hypothesis over another. 


6.5 Two-sample mean test using ggbetweenstats() method
We will use a visual of two-sample mean test on Math scores by gender using the ggbetweenstats() function

ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam_data,
  x = GENDER,
  y = MATHS,
  type ="np",
  messages = FALSE
)








x,y sets GENDER as the grouping variable ans MATHS scores as the outcome.
type chooses a non-parametric test due to assumptions of non-normality.
messages false means it suppresses extra messages/warnings from the statistical test output.
Interpretation: This plot compares maths score distributions between female and male students. Each violin shows the spread of scores with boxplots, individual data points,and summary statistics.


6.6 Oneway ANOVA Test using ggbetweenstats() method
We will use a visual for Oneway ANOVA test on English scores by race using the ggbetweenstats() function

ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam_data,
  x = RACE,
  y = ENGLISH,
  type ="p",
  mean.ci = TRUE,
  pairwise_comparisons = TRUE,
  pairwise.display = "s",
  p.adjust.method = "fdr",
  messages = FALSE
)








type chooses a parametric test for group comparison.
mean.ci TRUE displays confidence intervals around group means in the plot.
pairwise_comparisons TRUE run pairwise tests between groups.
pairwise.display “s” shows significance markers for pairwise comparisons directly on the plot. “ns” shows only non-significant and “all” shows everything.
p.adjust.method adjusts p-values using the false discovery rate method to control for multiple comparisons.
Interpretation: This plot compares English score distributions across racial groups. The statistical results above show a significant difference among groups (Welch’s F = 10.15,p ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁴), with Chinese and Others having higher mean scores than Indian and Malay, while the Bayesian metrics above confirm strong evidence supporting these group differences.

6.6.1 Summary of Tests
 
Summary of multiple pairwise comparison tests supported in ggbetweenstats 



6.7 Significant Test of Correlation using ggscatterstats() method
We will use a visual for Significant Test if Correlation between Maths and English scores using the ggscatterstats() function

ggscatterstats(
  data = exam_data,
  x = MATHS,
  y = ENGLISH,
  marginal = FALSE,
)








marginal FALSE disables the marginal plots, so only the main scatterplot with statistical results is displayed
Interpretation: This scatter plot shows a strong positive relationship between Maths and English scores, with most points clustering along the upward sloping regression line. The correlation coefficient 0.83 and extremely small p‑value statistically confirm that students who perform well in maths tend to also achieve high english scores.


6.8 Significant Test of Association (Dependence) using ggbarstats method
We will use cut() to bin the Maths scores inot a 4 class variables

exam1 <- exam_data %>%
  mutate(MATHS_bins =
          cut(MATHS,
              breaks = c(0,60,75,85,100))
)

Next, ggbarstats() is used to build a visual for the test of association

ggbarstats(exam1,
           x = MATHS_bins,
           y = GENDER)








Interpretation: This stacked bar chart compares Maths score distributions across Gender. The statistical results at the top show no significant difference in score proportions between genders, meaning both groups have similar performance patterns across the defined score ranges.

7 Visualizing Uncertainty
The use of graphics to represent uncertainty is a relatively recent development in statistical visualization. In this section, we will learn how to:

Draw error bars with ggplot2.

8 Getting started

8.1 Check, install and launch packages
For this section, we will work with several packages:

tidyverse is a collection of packages supporting the full data science workflow.
plotly is for building interactive plots.
gganimate is for creating animated graphics.
DT is for rendering interactive HTML tables.
crosstalk is to enable cross‑widget interactions such as linked brushing and filtering.
ggdist — for visualizing distributions and uncertainty.


pacman:::p_load(plotly, crosstalk, DT, ggdist, ggridges, colorspace, gganimate, tidyverse)



8.2 Visualizing the uncertainty of point estimates using ggplot2() methods
A point estimate is a single numerical summary, such as the mean. In contrast, uncertainty is conveyed through measures like the standard error, confidence intervals, or credible intervals.In this section, we will learn how to visualize uncertainty by plotting error bars of Maths scores across racial groups, using the exam tibble data frame.
To begin, the following code chunk will generate the required summary statistics.

my_sum <- exam_data %>%
  group_by(RACE) %>%
  summarise(
    n=n(),
    mean=mean(MATHS),
    sd=sd(MATHS)
    ) %>%
  mutate(se=sd/sqrt(n-1))

group_by() from dplyr is used to organize the data by the variable RACE, so calculations are done within each racial group.
summarise() then computes summary statistics for each group: the number of observations, the mean, and the standard deviation of Maths scores.
mutate() adds a new column that calculates the standard error of Maths scores for each racial group.
Finally, the results are stored as a tibble called my_sum, which holds the grouped summary table.

8.3 Plotting standard error bars of point estimates
We will plot the standard error bars of mean Maths score by Race using geom_errorbar()

ggplot(my_sum) +

    alpha = 0.9,
    linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(
    x = RACE, y = mean),
    stat = "identity",
    color = "pink",
    size = 1.5,
    alpha = 1) +

geom_errorbar section
aes(x = RACE, ymin = mean-se, ymax = mean+se) plots bars centered on the group mean, extending one s.e. above and below
width controls the horizontal width of the error bar caps
color sets the bar color

linewidth sets the line thickness
geom_point() adds points at the group means
geom_point section

8.4 Plotting Confidence Interval of Point Estimates

The plotThe code chunk













ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x = reorder(RACE, -mean),
        ymin = mean-1.96*se,
        ymax = mean+1.96*se),
    width = 0.2,
    color = "black",
    alpha = 0.9,
    linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(
    x = RACE, y = mean),
    stat = "identity",
    color = "pink",
    size = 1.5,
    alpha = 1) +
  labs(x = "Maths Score",
      title = "95% CI of Mean Maths Score by Race")
...reorder groups are reordered by descending mean score, instead of using RACE as its default
ymin , ymax plots 95% CI where the upper and lower limit bound formula is (mean ± 1.96 * se)
labs() updates the x-axis label and give title
The rest remains the same as in the earlier standard errors plot code





8.5 Visualizing the uncertainty of point estimates with interactive error bars
We will learn how to plot interactive error bars for the 99% CI of mean Maths score by Race shown below

The plotThe code chunk




















shared_df = SharedData$new(my_sum)

bscols(widths = c(4,8),
       ggplotly(ggplot(shared_df) +
                  geom_errorbar(aes(
                    x = reorder(RACE, -mean),
                    ymin = mean-2.58*se,
                    ymax = mean+2.58*se),
                    width = 0.2,
                    color = "black",
                    alpha = 0.9,
                    size = 0.5) +
                  geom_point(aes(
                    x = RACE,
                    y = mean,
                    text = paste("Race:", `RACE`,
                                 "<br>N:", `n`,
                                 "<br>Avg. Scores:", round(mean, digits = 2),
                                 round((mean-2.58*se), digits = 2), ",",
                                 round((mean+2.58*se), digits = 2),"]")),
                    stat = "identity",
                    color = "pink",
                    size = 1.5,
                    alpha = 1) +
                  xlab("Race") +
                  ylab("Average Scores") +
                  theme_minimal() +
                  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
                    angle=45, vjust=0.5, hjust=1)) +
                  ggtitle("99% Confidence Interval of Average /<br>Maths Scores by Race"),
                 tooltip = "text"
      ),
      DT::datatable(shared_df,
                    rownames = FALSE,
                    class = "compact",
                    width = "100%",
                    options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX=T),
                    colnames = c("No of pupils", "Avg Scores", "Std Dev", "Std error")) %>%
        formatRound(columns=c('mean', 'sd', 'se'), digits =2))
Code explanation divided into different chunks:

shared_df creates a shared data object from my_sum. This allows linking between the plot and the datatable and enhance filtering to be synchronized
bscols arranges two components side by side

reorder() orders groups by descending mean
ymin , ymax plots 99% CI where the upper and lower limit bound formula is (mean ± 2.58 * se)
text shows RACE, sample size(n), average scores and CI bounds
angle rotates x-axis labels 45° for readability
tooltip text ensures the custom tooltip is shown in the interactive plot
Interactive datatable
It displays the same data in an interactive HTML table
rownames FALSE sets no row names
class compact style
width 100% sets to full width
formatRound rounds numeric columns (mean, sd, se) to 2 decimal places





8.6 Visualizing Uncertainty using ggdist() package
ggdist is an R package that extends ggplot2 with specialized geoms and stats for visualizing distributions and uncertainty. It supports both frequentist and Bayesian approaches, built on the idea that uncertainty can be understood through distribution visualization:

In frequentist models, we can display confidence distributions or bootstrap distributions (refering to vignette("freq-uncertainty-vis")).
In Bayesian models, we visualize probability distributions, often using the tidybayes package, which builds on top of ggdist. 



8.7 Visualizing the uncertainty of point estimates using stat_pointinterval() method
We will use stat_pointinterval() of ggdist to build a visual for displaying distribution of Maths Scores by Race

exam_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE,
             y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval() +
  labs(
    title = "Visualizing Confidence Intervals of Mean Maths Score",
    subtitle = "Mean Point + Multiple-interval Plot"
  )

                     .point = median,

10 Funnel Plots for Fair Comparisons
A funnel plot is a specialized visualization tool designed to support fair comparisons across outlets, stores, or business units. In this section we will learn how to

create funnel plots using the funnelPlotR package
build static funnel plots with ggplot2
develop interactive funnel plots by combining plotly and ggplot2


10.1 Check, install and load packages

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, FunnelPlotR, plotly, knitr)

readr is for importing csv into R
FunnelPlotR is for creating a funnel plot
knitr is for building static html table


10.2 Importing Data
In this part of the exercise, we will work with the COVID‑19_DKI_Jakarta dataset. The focus is on comparing the cumulative COVID‑19 cases and deaths across sub‑districts (i.e. kelurahan) in DKI Jakarta as of 31 July 2021.
The following code chunk imports the dataset into R and stores it as a tibble data frame named covid19.

covid19 <- read_csv("../data/COVID-19_DKI_Jakarta.csv") %>% mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

We will show the table as an interactive html table by using the DT package

library(DT)
datatable(covid19)





It created a searachable and sortable table.


10.3 FunnelPlotR methods
The FunnelPlotR package builds funnel plots using ggplot2. To generate a plot, we need to provide a numerator (events of interest, a denominator (the relevant population) and a grouping variable. The key customization options include:

limit sets confidence (95% or 99%)
label_outliers sets whether outliers are labeled (TRUE/FALSE)
poisson_limits adds Poisson distributions limits
OD_adjust applies overdispersion adjustments
xrange and yrange defines axis ranges, functioning like a zoom
Other aesthetic components to customize title, axis labels and other visual details



10.4 Creating a basic plot with FunnelPlotR methods
This code chunk displays a funnel plot object with 267 points where there is no outlier. Plot is adjusted overdispersion.

The plotCode explanation



funnel_plot(
  .data = covid19,
  numerator = Positive,
  denominator = Death,
  group = `Sub-district`
)








A funnel plot object with 267 points of which 0 are outliers. 
Plot is adjusted for overdispersion. 




numerator = Positive defines the number of positive cases
denominator = Death defines the number of deaths.
group sets the grouping variable as sub-district.
Improvements suggested are adding plot limits, label outliers, adjust for overdispersion, zoom into range, and add titles and or labels
By default data_type = “SR” in FunnelPlotR means the plot is built for indirectly standardised ratios (SR).





10.5 FunnelPlotR data_type Controls

“SR” is the default data_type argument where it stands for Standardised Ratios. It compares observed events against expected values adjusted for case mix, rather than raw proportions or simple count ratios.
“PR” stands for Proportions. It uses numerator/denominator directly as a proportion.
“RC” is Ratios of Counts. It compares raw counts between groups. it may be useful for comparing absolute event counts across units.


10.5.1 Makeover 1
We will change our data_type to PR as it is more appropriate in this case. Moreover, we will specify the axis ranges.

funnel_plot(
  .data = covid19,
  numerator = Death,
  denominator = Positive,
  group = `Sub-district`,
  data_type = "PR",
  xrange = c(0,6500),
  yrange = c(0, 0.05)
)








A funnel plot object with 267 points of which 7 are outliers. 
Plot is adjusted for overdispersion. 


From the plot above, there is still room for improvement


10.5.2 Makeover 2
In the second makeover, we will give a title for the plot and the axis. We will remove the default label outliers feature as shown in the code below.

funnel_plot(
  .data = covid19,
  numerator = Death,
  denominator = Positive,
  group = `Sub-district`,
  data_type = "PR",
  xrange = c(0,6500),
  yrange = c(0, 0.05),
  label = NA,
  title = "Cumulative COVID-19 Fatality Rate by Cumulative Total Number of COVID-19 Positive Cases",
  x_label = "Cumulative COVID-19 Positive Cases",
  y_label = "Cumulative Fatality Rate"
)








A funnel plot object with 267 points of which 7 are outliers. 
Plot is adjusted for overdispersion. 





10.6 Funnel Plot for Fair Visual Comparison using ggplot2 methods
In this section, we will construct funnel plots step by step with ggplot2. The goal is to strengthen our ability to customize specialized visualizations such as funnel plots, while deepening our working knowledge of ggplot2.


10.7 Computing the basic derived fields
To build a funnel plot from scratch, we need to calculate two key values for each group.

Cumulative Death Rate - this is the proportion of deaths relative to the population at risk.
Standard Error of Death Rate - the s.e. quantifies uncertainty around the death rate estimate. The formula for binomial standard error for a proportion is s.e = sqrt((p*(1-p))/n)


df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death/Positive) %>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate*(1-rate)) / (Positive))) %>%
  filter(rate > 0)

filter(rate>0) keeps only rows where the death rate is greater than zero.
Next, fit.mean is computed using the code chunk below

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1/df$rate.se^2)

weighted.mean computes a mean value where each observation is given a weight
df$rate is the vector of death rates for each sub-district
1/df$rate.se^2 is the wights. This is the inverse variance weighting.


10.8 Computing lower and upper limit for 95% and 99.9%
The code chunk below calculates the lower and upper limits for 95% and 99.9% confidence interval

number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1) 
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
dfCI <- data.frame(number.ll95, number.ul95, number.ll999,
                   number.ul999, number.seq, fit.mean)

number.seq creates a sequence of integers from 1 up to maximum number of positive cases. This serves as possible denominators for which confidence limits will be calculated
number.ll95 and number.ll999 calculates the lower 95% and 99.9% confidence limit for each sample size.
number.ul95 and number.up999 calculates the upper 95% and 99.9% confidence limit for each sample size.

z-score for the 95% is 1.96 and for 99.9% is 3.29

dfCI combines all calculated limits and the sequence to one dataframe. This will be used to draw the funnel plot curves around the pooled mean.


10.9 Plotting a static funnel plot using ggplot2 method

The plotThe code chunkCode explaination













p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Positive, y = rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(label=`Sub-district`), 
             alpha=0.4) +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ll95), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40", 
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ul95), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40", 
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ll999), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ul999), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(data = dfCI, 
             aes(yintercept = fit.mean), 
             size = 0.4, 
             colour = "grey40") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,0.05)) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = -0.13, label = "95%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + 
  annotate("text", x = 4.5, y = -0.18, label = "99%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + 
  ggtitle("Cumulative Fatality Rate by Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") +
  xlab("Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") + 
  ylab("Cumulative Fatality Rate") +
  theme_light() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size=12),
        legend.position = c(0.91,0.85), 
        legend.title = element_text(size=7),
        legend.text = element_text(size=7),
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey60", linetype = "dotted"),
        legend.key.height = unit(0.3, "cm"))
p


p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Positive, y = rate)) +
Initializes a ggplot using df and sets x-axis to be Positive cases while y-axis is the fatality rate
  geom_point(aes(label=`Sub-district`), alpha=0.4) +
Plots each sub-district as a point, Sub-district column as labels, and semi transparent point
  geom_line(data = dfCI, aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ll95), size = 0.4, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") + 
  geom_line(data = dfCI, aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ul95), size = 0.4, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
Draws the lower and upper 95% confidence limit curve in dashed grey line
  geom_line(data = dfCI, aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ll999), size = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, aes(x = number.seq, y = number.ul999), size = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
Draws the lower and upper 99.9% confidence limit curve in solid grey line
  geom_hline(data = dfCI, aes(yintercept = fit.mean), size = 0.4, colour = "grey40") +
Adds a horizontal line at the pooled mean fatality rate and serves as the central reference line
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,0.05)) +
Restricts the y-axis to values between 0 and 0.05. This draws a plot only on the relevant range of fatality rates
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = -0.13, label = "95%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + 
  annotate("text", x = 4.5, y = -0.18, label = "99%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
Adds text annotations “95%” and “99%” near the plot to indicate confidence bands. It is positioned manually with x and y coordinates.
  ggtitle("Cumulative Fatality Rate by Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") +
  xlab("Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") + 
  ylab("Cumulative Fatality Rate") +
Sets the plot title and axis labels
  theme_light() +
Applies a light theme for the plot background
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size=12),
        legend.position = c(0.91,0.85), 
        legend.title = element_text(size=7),
        legend.text = element_text(size=7),
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey60", linetype = "dotted"),
        legend.key.height = unit(0.3, "cm"))
This chunk customizes few theme elements: title font size, legend position in top right corner, legend text and title sizes, legend background with dotted grey border, legend key height





10.10 Interactive Funnel Plot using plotly and ggplot2
Next, we can upgrade the static plot to an interactive one by using ggplotly() from plotly R package. The code chunk below is the demo on how to use the function

fp_ggplotly <- ggplotly(p,
  tooltip = c("label", 
              "x", 
              "y"))
fp_ggplotly

title: Visual Analytics of a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Insurers often carry underperforming portfolios where the root causes of poor profitability and high volatility remain unknown. This study applies visual analytics to a real-world motor vehicle insurance portfolio from a Spanish non-life insurance company, covering policy years 2022–2024. With 354,140 policy-year observations and 47 variables spanning policy characteristics, driver and vehicle attributes, premiums, claims, incurred costs, and exposure, this dataset provides a rich foundation for exploring the loss drivers that underpin portfolio profitability.
The research questions are:

How are key portfolio variables distributed across numerical and categorical dimensions?
Which factors are statistically associated with higher claim frequency, loss severity, or loss ratio — the principal measures of insurance profitability and volatility?

title: Visual Analytics of a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Insurers often carry underperforming portfolios where the root causes of poor profitability and high volatility remain unknown. This study applies visual analytics to a real-world motor vehicle insurance portfolio from a Spanish non-life insurance company, covering policy years 2022–2024. With 354,140 policy-year observations and 47 variables spanning policy characteristics, driver and vehicle attributes, premiums, claims, incurred costs, and exposure, this dataset provides a rich foundation for exploring the loss drivers that underpin portfolio profitability.
The research questions are:

How are key portfolio variables distributed across numerical and categorical dimensions?
Which factors are statistically associated with higher claim frequency, loss severity, or loss ratio — the principal measures of insurance profitability and volatility?

3.2 Cleaning & Recoding


Show code
mip <- raw %>%
  # 1. Drop duplicate rows (same insured_id, year, policy
  distinct() %>%

  # 2. Recode categorical variables as factors with descriptive labels 
  mutate(
    # Policy type (coverage breadth, low → high)
    policy_type = factor(
      policy_type,
      levels = c("TP", "TPG", "CC", "COMP_E", "COMP_N"),
      labels = c(
        "Third-party\n(TP)",
        "Third-party\n+ Glass (TPG)",
        "Combined\nCoverage (CC)",
        "Comprehensive\nwith Excess",
        "Comprehensive\nNo Excess"
      )
    ),

    policy_status  = factor(policy_status,  levels = c("A","C"),
                            labels = c("Active","Cancelled")),
    business_type  = factor(business_type,  levels = c("NB","P"),
                            labels = c("New Business","Portfolio")),
    payment_frequency = factor(payment_frequency, levels = c("A","S","Q"),
                               labels = c("Annual","Semi-annual","Quarterly")),
    bonus_score    = factor(bonus_score, levels = c("G","N","B"),
                            labels = c("Good","Neutral","Bad"),
                            ordered = TRUE),
    fuel_type      = factor(fuel_type,   levels = c("G","D"),
                            labels = c("Gasoline","Diesel")),
    municipality_type = factor(municipality_type, levels = c("I","C","IS"),
                               labels = c("Inland","Coastal","Islands")),
    circulation_area  = factor(circulation_area, levels = c("U","R"),
                               labels = c("Urban","Rural")),
    year = as.integer(year)
  ) %>%

  # 3. Derive actuarial risk metrics and categorical groupings
  mutate(
    # Loss Ratio: how much of premium is consumed by claims costs
    loss_ratio = if_else(
      total_premium > 0,
      total_incurred / total_premium,
      NA_real_
    ),

    # Claim frequency per policy year (normalised by exposure) to indicate how often claims occur per unit of risk
    claim_freq = if_else(
      total_exposure > 0,
      total_claims / total_exposure,
      NA_real_
    ),

    # Average claim severity (cost per claim, 0 when no claims) to highlight how expensive individual claims are
    claim_severity = if_else(
      total_claims > 0,
      total_incurred / total_claims,
      NA_real_
    ),

    # Pure premium (incurred per unit of exposure) used in pricing models to set fair premiums
    pure_premium = if_else(
      total_exposure > 0,
      total_incurred / total_exposure,
      NA_real_
    ),

    # Has-claim flag (TRUE if policy had at least one claim, FALSE otherwise)
    had_claim = total_claims > 0,

    # Driver grouping
    driver_age_band = cut(
      driver_age,
      breaks = c(17, 24, 34, 44, 54, 64, Inf),
      labels = c("18-24","25-34","35-44","45-54","55-64","65+"),
      right  = TRUE
    ),

    # Vehicle age grouping
    vehicle_age_band = cut(
      vehicle_age,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 5, 10, 20, 35, Inf),
      labels = c("0-5 yrs","6-10 yrs","11-20 yrs","21-35 yrs","35+ yrs"),
      right  = TRUE
    )
  )

cat("Cleaned dataset dimensions:", nrow(mip), "rows ×", ncol(mip), "columns\n")

This transformation turns raw claim and premium data into interpretable acturial measures such as

profitability via loss ratio and pure premium
volatility via claim frequency and severity
segmentation via driver and vehivle age groupings

Together, these metrics allow us to profile risk drivers and compare performance across policyholder groups

text:
4.1 Numerical Variables

4.1.1 Driver Age Distribution
A half-eye plot with embedded statistical summaries is chosen to balance distribution insight with summary statistics. The half-eye plot shows the full distribution shape to see skewness, added with median and mean as reference lines to make it easy in comparing central tendency measures. Implemented with ggdist stat_halfeye method, it helps to profile driver age, a critical risk factor in motor insurance.


Show code
p1 <- mip %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = driver_age)) +
  stat_halfeye(
    aes(y = 0),
    fill = "#4E79A7",
    alpha = 0.7,
    point_interval = mean_qi,
    slab_colour = "white",
    slab_linewidth = 0.3,
    normalize = "all"
  ) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(driver_age)),
             colour = "#E15759", linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(driver_age)),
             colour = "#59A14F", linewidth = 0.8, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = mean(mip$driver_age) + 1, y = 0.75,
           label = paste0("Mean: ", round(mean(mip$driver_age), 1)),
           hjust = 0, colour = "#E15759", size = 3.5) +
  annotate("text", x = median(mip$driver_age) - 1, y = 0.65,
           label = paste0("Median: ", round(median(mip$driver_age), 1)),
           hjust = 1, colour = "#59A14F", size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(20, 90, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.1))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Driver Age Distribution",
    subtitle = "Half-eye plot with mean (red dashed) and median (green dotted)",
    x        = "Driver Age (years)",
    y        = NULL,
    caption  = paste0("n = ", scales::comma(nrow(mip)))
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

p1








Figure 1






Insight: Driver age follows an approximately normal distribution centred around 49 years, with a slight right skew. The high representation of middle-aged drivers (40-60) reflects the portfolio’s focus on experienced policyholders. The relatively thin tail of young drivers (18-25) indicates limited exposure to high-risk segments.



4.1.2 Vehicle Age Distribution
Vehicle age is a key risk driver in motor insurance. Older vehicles may have different claim frequencies and severities compared to newer ones, so understanding the distribution is essential.
This method is selected because it combines histogram with density plot, implemented by using geom_histogram and geom_density function. It’s applied to profile vehicle age. From this plot, we aim to reveal whether the plot is skewed toward newer or older vehicles, identify clusters that may drive claim behaviour and provide intuitive visual summary of vehicle age distribution.


Show code
mip %>%
  drop_na(vehicle_age) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = vehicle_age)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)),
                 binwidth = 2, fill = "#76B7B2", colour = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_density(colour = "#4E79A7", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 70, 10)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Vehicle Age Distribution",
    subtitle = "Histogram with density overlay (bin width = 2 years)",
    x        = "Vehicle Age (years)",
    y        = "Density",
    caption  = paste0("n = ", scales::comma(sum(!is.na(mip$vehicle_age))))
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Figure 2






Insight: Vehicle age is distributed from 0 to 68 years, dominated by mid-aged vehicles. The long right tail suggests the insurer covers many older vehicles, which may present higher mechanical risk and lower residual insured values.



4.1.3 Total Premium Distribution
Premium distribution is central to understanding portfolio profitability and risk concentration. Outliers may represent large corporate policies or unusual contracts that skew averages.
This dual‑view technique is selected to balance transparency by showing outliers with interpretability by focusing on the bulk of the data. Implemented via geom_histogram and patchwork, it’s applied here to profile premium levels in the portfolio. We want to reveal whether most policies cluster at lower premium levels while a few extreme cases dominate the tail. It helps to decide whether to model premiums with or without outliers, depending on whether those large policies are typical or exceptional.


Show code
p_full <- mip %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = total_premium)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#F28E2B", colour = "white", bins = 80, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(prefix = "€")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Full Range", x = "Total Premium (€)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

q99 <- quantile(mip$total_premium, 0.99)

p_trim <- mip %>%
  filter(total_premium <= q99) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_premium)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#F28E2B", colour = "white", bins = 80, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(prefix = "€")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Trimmed to 99th Percentile",
       subtitle = paste0("(≤ €", scales::comma(round(q99))),
       x = "Total Premium (€)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

(p_full | p_trim) +
  plot_annotation(
    title   = "Total Premium Distribution",
    caption = paste0("n = ", scales::comma(nrow(mip)))
  )








Figure 3






Insight: The total premium is heavily right-skewed. The majority of policies generate premiums below €1,000, while a long tail of high-value contracts. When trimmed to the 99th percentile, the distribution shows a dense cluster below roughtly €1,000 as well, confirming that it is dominated by standard-risk policies. This skew is typical in commercial motor portfolios where a small minority of high-risk or high-value vehicles attract significantly higher premiums.



4.1.4 Claim Severity Distribution
We will plot a visualiation for the distribution of claim severity, referring to the average cost per claim for policies that had at least one claim. It uses a histogram with a density overlay, trimmed to the 99th percentile to focus on typical claim behaviour. Understanding its distribution helps model expected losses and detect heavy‑tailed risk patterns.We want to see whether claim costs cluster at lower amounts or not and also to identify potential heavy-tailed behaviour that may require adjustments.


Show code
q999 <- quantile(mip$claim_severity, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)
n_claims <- sum(mip$had_claim, na.rm = TRUE)

severity_data <- mip |>
  filter(had_claim) |>
  drop_na(claim_severity) |>
  filter(claim_severity <= q999)

# Compute histogram bins manually so density overlay aligns exactly
hist_obj  <- hist(severity_data$claim_severity, breaks = 100, plot = FALSE)
dens_obj  <- density(severity_data$claim_severity, from = 0, to = q999)

plot_ly() |>
  # Histogram bars (density scale)
  add_bars(
    x       = hist_obj$mids,
    y       = hist_obj$density,
    width   = diff(hist_obj$breaks),
    marker  = list(
      color = "rgba(225, 87, 89, 0.8)",   # #E15759 with alpha
      line  = list(color = "white", width = 0.5)
    ),
    name       = "Density",
    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "Severity: €%{x:,.0f}<br>",
      "Density: %{y:.6f}<extra></extra>"
    )
  ) |>
  # Density curve overlay
  add_lines(
    x    = dens_obj$x,
    y    = dens_obj$y,
    line = list(color = "#59A14F", width = 2),
    name = "Density curve",
    hovertemplate = paste0(
      "Severity: €%{x:,.0f}<br>",
      "Density: %{y:.6f}<extra></extra>"
    )
  ) |>
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = paste0(
        "Claim Severity Distribution",
        "<br><sup>Policies with ≥ 1 claim, trimmed to 99th percentile",
        " | n = ", scales::comma(n_claims), " claims</sup>"
      ),
      font = list(size = 14)
    ),
    xaxis = list(title = "Claim Severity (€ per claim)", tickformat = "€,.0f", range= c(0, q999)
    ),
    yaxis  = list(title = "Density"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0.65, y = 0.95),
    margin = list(t = 80, b = 60)
  )








Figure 4





Insight: Claim severity is strongly right-skewed with most claims under €5,000. The long tail reflects the occasional high-cost event (serious injury liability, total vehicle loss), where a few costly clains drive volatility and profitability risk. ## Categorical Variables



4.1.5 Policy Type
We will see the composition of policy type. The implementation uses count() to tally policies by type, calculate percentages for context. The result give us a quick lovk of how the insurer’s business is distributed across product lines.


Show code

  mutate(
    pct  = n / sum(n),
    label = paste0(scales::comma(n), "\n(", scales::percent(pct, accuracy = 0.1), ")")

  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(policy_type, n, .desc = TRUE), y = n, fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +

Insight: CC dominate the portfolio at roughly half of all observations, followed by CC_E. This mix signals an insurer serving both high-coverage and budget-conscious segments simultaneously. This will typically stabilizes profitability but may limit growth in lower‑premium segments.



4.1.6 Bonus Score Business Type & Payment Frequency
The bar charts allow direct comparison of counts and proportions across the categories. We will use make_bar() function to count observations per category, compute percentages and annotate each bar with its share of the portfolio. We want to see the categorical segmentation whether it is dominated by these categories. These findings are crticial for understanding customer behavioru, retension and risk exposure.


Show code
make_bar <- function(data, var, title, palette = "Set1") {
  data %>%
    count({{ var }}, name = "n") %>%
    mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = {{ var }}, y = n, fill = {{ var }})) +
    geom_col(width = 0.65, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(pct, accuracy = 0.1)),
              vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma,
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +

5.1 Loss Ratio by Policy Type
The half‑eye plots of loss ratio by policy type provide a clear application for portfolio profitability analysis. text:
5.6 Temporal Trends: Loss Ratio by Year
Line charts with grouped categories are ideal for showing temporal trends and highlighting how portfolio loss ratios evolve across years. This enables insurers to track whether specific products are improving or deteriorating over time to assess sustainability of pricing and adjust portfolio mix.


Show code
trend_data <- mip %>%
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio), total_premium > 0) %>%
  group_by(year, policy_type) %>%
  summarise(
    portfolio_lr = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium),
    n            = n(),
    .groups      = "drop"
  )

set2_colours <- RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(n = nlevels(trend_data$policy_type), 
                                          name = "Set2")
policy_types <- levels(trend_data$policy_type)

p <- plot_ly()

# Add one trace per policy type to match grouped ggplot lines
for (i in seq_along(policy_types)) {
  pt  <- policy_types[i]
  df_i <- filter(trend_data, policy_type == pt)

  p <- p %>%
    add_trace(
      data       = df_i,
      x          = ~year,
      y          = ~portfolio_lr,
      type       = "scatter",
      mode       = "lines+markers",
      name       = pt,
      line       = list(color = set2_colours[i], width = 2.5),
      marker     = list(
        color  = set2_colours[i],
        size   = ~scales::rescale(n, to = c(6, 18)),  
        opacity = 0.8
      ),
      text       = ~paste0(
        "Policy Type: ",  policy_type,
        "<br>Year: ",     year,
        "<br>Loss Ratio: ", scales::percent(portfolio_lr, accuracy = 0.1),
        "<br>Policies: ",   scales::comma(n)
      ),
      hoverinfo  = "text"
    )
}

p %>%
  # Break-even reference line
  add_segments(
    x    = min(trend_data$year) - 0.1,
    xend = max(trend_data$year) + 0.1,
    y    = 1, yend = 1,
    line = list(color = "red", dash = "dash", width = 1.5),
    hoverinfo  = "none",
    showlegend = FALSE,
    inherit    = FALSE
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = paste0(
        "Portfolio Loss Ratio Trend by Policy Type (2022–2024)",
        "<br><sup>Aggregate loss ratio per year; red dashed line = break-even (100%)</sup>"
      ),
      font = list(size = 14)
    ),
    xaxis = list(
      title      = "Calendar Year",
      tickvals   = c(2022, 2023, 2024),   
      tickformat = "d"
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      title      = "Loss Ratio",
      tickformat = ".0%",                 
      dtick      = 0.2,                   
      range      = list(0, 1.2)
    ),
    legend = list(title = list(text = "<b>Policy Type</b>")),
    margin = list(t = 80)
  )








Figure 15





Insight: Comprehensive policies (COMP_E and COMP_N) have tracked close to or above the break-even loss ratio in recent years, signalling potential pricing inadequacy. Third-party policies show more stable loss ratios. The upward trend in 2024 for some segments warrants investigation, it could reflect claims inflation (repair costs rising faster than premiums) or portfolio deterioration from aggressive growth.

  group_by(vehicle_brand, policy_type) %>%
  summarise(
    total_prem = sum(total_premium),
    mean_lr    = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium),
    n_policies = n(),
    .groups    = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(n_policies >= 500)

brand_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(
    area   = total_prem,
    fill   = mean_lr,
    label  = vehicle_brand,
    subgroup = policy_type
  )) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(colour = "darkgrey", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_text(
    place    = "topleft",
    colour   = "white",
    alpha    = 0.7,
    fontface = "bold",
    size     = 9,
    grow     = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    colour   = "darkblue",
    alpha    = 0.9,
    place    = "centre",
    size     = 8,
    grow     = FALSE,
    reflow   = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low      = "#59A14F",
    mid      = "lightyellow",
    high     = "#E15759",
    midpoint = 1,
    name     = "Loss Ratio",
    labels   = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Premium Concentration by Vehicle Brand and Policy Type",
    subtitle = "Tile area = total premium; colour = portfolio loss ratio (green = profitable)",
    caption  = "Brands/policy type combinations with < 500 policies excluded"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Figure 18






Insight: The treemap shows that brands like Mercedes, Volkswagen, and BMW dominate premium share, yet profitability differs by policy type: Comprehensive No Excess tends to show higher loss ratios (less profitable), whereas Third‑party + Glass and Comprehensive with Excess are generally greener, signaling better underwriting results.

This sina plot is superior to simple boxplots for capturing heterogeneity in pure premium across bonus score groups.T he implementation filters and caps extreme values, applies a log transformation for scale stability, and overlays mean ± 1 SD error bars to balance detail with summary statistic. We can assess how historical claims behavior (bonus score) translates into pure premium differences

set.seed(42)

mip %>%
  filter(

  geom_sina(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8, maxwidth = 0.7) +
  stat_summary(

text:
5.11 Premium vs Incurred Across Policy Types
This plot allows simultaneous visualization of the relationship between total premium and total incurred across multiple policy types. A break‑even diagonal line is added to provides a clear profitability benchmark. We aim insurers to detect product‑specific profitability patterns also to identify clusters of unprofitable policies.


Show code
set.seed(123)

scatter_data <- mip %>%
  filter(had_claim, total_premium > 0, total_incurred > 0,
         total_premium  <= quantile(total_premium,  0.99),
         total_incurred <= quantile(total_incurred, 0.99)) %>%
  slice_sample(n = 20000) %>%
  mutate(
    lr_capped = pmin(loss_ratio, 3),          
    hover_text = paste0(
      "Policy Type: ",    policy_type,
      "<br>Premium: €",   scales::comma(round(total_premium, 0)),
      "<br>Incurred: €",  scales::comma(round(total_incurred, 0)),
      "<br>Loss Ratio: ", scales::percent(loss_ratio, accuracy = 0.1)
    )
  )

# Diverging colour scale matching scale_colour_gradient2
# low=#59A14F (LR=0), mid=#EEEEEE (LR=1), high=#E15759 (LR=3)
lr_colorscale <- list(
  list(0,    "#59A14F"),
  list(1/3,  "#EEEEEE"),   # midpoint at LR = 1 → position 1/3 of [0,3]
  list(1,    "#E15759")
)

policy_types <- levels(scatter_data$policy_type)
n_types      <- length(policy_types)

# Build subplot grid (same layout as facet_wrap)
n_cols  <- 3
n_rows  <- ceiling(n_types / n_cols)

subplot_list <- lapply(seq_along(policy_types), function(i) {

  pt   <- policy_types[i]
  df_i <- filter(scatter_data, policy_type == pt)

  # Break-even line spans the data range of this facet
  ax_max <- max(max(df_i$total_premium), max(df_i$total_incurred))

  plot_ly(df_i,
    x         = ~total_premium,
    y         = ~total_incurred,
    text      = ~hover_text,
    hoverinfo = "text",
    type      = "scatter",
    mode      = "markers",
    marker    = list(
      color    = ~lr_capped,
      colorscale = lr_colorscale,
      cmin     = 0,
      cmax     = 3,
      size     = 4,
      opacity  = 0.3,
      colorbar = if (i == n_types)            # show colorbar once only
        list(
          title      = "Loss<br>Ratio",
          tickformat = ".0%",
          tickvals   = c(0, 1, 2, 3),
          ticktext   = c("0%", "100%", "200%", "≥300%"),
          len        = 0.5
        )
      else list(showscale = FALSE)
    ),
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) %>%
    # Break-even diagonal
    add_segments(
      x    = 0,    xend = ax_max,
      y    = 0,    yend = ax_max,
      line = list(color = "red", dash = "dash", width = 1),
      hoverinfo  = "none",
      showlegend = FALSE,
      inherit    = FALSE
    ) %>%
    layout(
      annotations = list(list(
        text      = paste0("<b>", pt, "</b>"),
        x         = 0.5, y = 1.05,
        xref      = "paper", yref = "paper",
        showarrow = FALSE,
        font      = list(size = 11)
      )),
      xaxis = list(tickformat = "€,.0f", range= c(0, 1000), dtick = 200, title = ""),
      yaxis = list(tickformat = "€,.0f", title = "")
    )
})

subplot(
  subplot_list,
  nrows       = n_rows,
  shareX      = FALSE,
  shareY      = FALSE,
  titleX      = FALSE,
  titleY      = FALSE,
  margin      = 0.07
) %>%
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = paste0(
        "Total Premium vs Total Incurred by Policy Type",
        "<br><sup>Red diagonal = break-even line; points above are unprofitable",
        " | 20,000 random sample; axes trimmed to 99th percentile</sup>"
      ),
      font = list(size = 13)
    ),
    annotations = list(
      # Shared x-axis label
      list(text = "Total Premium (€)", x = 0.5,  y = -0.05,
           xref = "paper", yref = "paper", showarrow = FALSE,
           font = list(size = 12)),
      # Shared y-axis label
      list(text = "Total Incurred (€)", x = -0.06, y = 0.5,
           xref = "paper", yref = "paper", showarrow = FALSE,
           textangle = -90, font = list(size = 12))
    ),
    margin = list(l = 80, b = 70, t = 90)
  )








Figure 20





Insight: The plot highlights how coverage generosity correlates with claim cost, guiding underwriting strategy and pricing optimization.The red diagonal marks the break‑even line points above it are unprofitable. Third‑party (TP) and Third‑party + Glass (TPG) policies cluster below the line, indicating strong profitability.
